102.canonical: Treat tool-description augmentation as useful but not universal or free: apply it adaptively by domain and model while budgeting for higher execution steps and token use and watching for regressions.

110.canonical: Write tool descriptions with all core quality components present and viable: purpose, usage guidance, limitations, parameter details, and self-sufficient prose, with examples only supplementing the description.

112.canonical: Keep tool descriptions accurate and precise: state only implemented behavior, concrete constraints, parameter meanings, and boundaries, while removing ambiguous, contradictory, or self-referential wording.

116.canonical: Use source-code grounding as a reliability safeguard for tool-description faithfulness, especially for behavior- and input-tied components, while not assuming it will always improve task success.

49.canonical: Use reference trajectories for solvability checks and post-hoc diagnostics only; score pass/fail by grounded claims so valid alternative paths are not penalized.

60.canonical: Structure diagnostic judging around the verified evidence trace, expected claims, missed claims, and actual behavior so failures are localized without penalizing alternative valid plans.

61.canonical: Use one shared failure-mode vocabulary for human reviewers and automated diagnostic judges, assigning the primary root-cause mode plus contributing modes with explicit confidence and disambiguation rules.

82.canonical: Before trusting poor eval scores, verify that the tasks and graders are fair, unambiguous, and correctly configured so failures reflect agent behavior rather than broken evaluation.

85.canonical: Treat evaluations as routine development artifacts: define realistic capability evals early, iterate on them like unit tests, and use them to make progress and unstated expectations visible.
